title: DAY OF RECKONING FOR UNIS
full_text:
The business downturn in NSW and Victoria is intensifying and spreading into other states. It means young people entering the workforce in 2027 will face a jobs market not seen in Australia since 2007-09 and the early 1990s.
This decline is fanning support for the Liberals and One Nation. Our young people are totally unprepared for what is ahead because, leaving aside Covid-19, for almost all their lives there has been a shortage of labour.
We were headed into tougher times before the budget, but the Chalmers budget – which appears to have been driven by the hard-left forces in Treasury – has intensified the impact of the downturn.
And artificial intelligence is making this downturn different from anything we have seen in half a century.
Enterprises down to single traders are now using artificial intelligence to improve productivity. Over the weekend I was in the company of a sole trader with contractors who has found a niche in the renovation market and is managing his operational back office via AI, which is transforming the economics of his business. In any economy where productivity starts to improve and there is no growth, the end result is higher unemployment.
And the fate of our younger people has been made even worse because our universities have management structures that are totally inappropriate for the new Australian environment.
Vice-chancellors’ decision-making is subject to endless committees and bureaucracies and, partly as a result, they were unable to stop the rise in antisemitism. While they were dealing with campus chaos, they did not change their teaching to prepare the 2026 final-year students for the AI-dominated world they were going to move into in 2027.
The boards of our universities need to step in and begin to reorganise their universities so they can prepare students for a totally different world to the one university professors have been used to.
The students must understand how to use AI when they enter the workforce. Universities in the future are going to be marked on the salaries and the employment engagement percentages that their exiting students obtain.
Meanwhile, countless Australian businesses now are battling rises in costs of more than 10 per cent, led by wages, power, rent and increasing regulations.
They are having great difficulty passing those extra charges on unless they have a product that is doing well or they gain a break over their opponent, either using AI or other means. Most are not hiring and large numbers know they must reduce staff.
But many medium and smaller-sized businesses find that they simply don’t have the cash to pay retrenchment benefits so they are hanging on, hoping people will leave. Businesses that can’t pay needed retrenchment bills often collapse and everyone’s job is lost.
The government and unions think they can put a “cork” into enterprises to stop AI-driven events. But “AI-corked” enterprises will simply be destroyed by their “uncorked” rivals.
Remember that AI is akin to the introduction of electricity. If a couple of centuries ago governments were stupid enough to restrain enterprises from using electricity, those enterprises would quickly be put out of business, and that is exactly what will happen if Anthony Albanese goes too far.
In any downturn people delay payments and what has surprised me about this one is that accountants are finding their clients are taking longer to pay bills.
Naturally, this is not easy for accountants dealing with long-standing clients because they know exactly what the problem is.
There are of course areas of the economy that are still doing well. Contractors in government-backed infrastructure projects and the NDIS are enjoying life. Increasingly, big construction projects are being dominated by the CFMEU, which explodes the costs, but the projects continue to proceed. The Queensland government, facing an Olympic problem, plans to pass legislation to curb the power of the CFMEU and related organised crime. If it fails, it will either be saddled with a huge increase in Olympic costs or the Olympics will be in jeopardy.
In NSW the powerful bureaucracies in state and local governments make building in that state prohibitively costly. And in Victoria large projects have become infested with crime and corruption. Nevertheless, these projects reward employees and “approved contractors” very well.
But new housing jobs can’t pay the same money because the selling prices are too low and values are falling in the existing home auction market. So we have an enormous residential building industry where there are hard times despite shortages. Now back to universities. In the past, the job of making students “work-ready” was undertaken by the private sector, particularly large enterprises.
But bad practices in the accounting profession and the advent of AI in almost all professions means that the tasks that made young people “work-ready” are no longer required.
Our universities have to make our young people “work-ready”. That means enormous change in the way they operate and, given that the boards and chief executives don’t have the same sort of powers that a public company possesses, it becomes very difficult for universities to adapt to such a fundamental change. But those that don’t adapt face a torrid time. One can only hope that issues like antisemitism, which have scarred the reputation of universities like ANU, Sydney and Melbourne, will be stripped aside by the need to actually adapt to a new environment. But don’t bet on it. But for universities that don’t adapt the retrenchments will be unprecedented.
